item.title: Britain Approves New Gas Drilling in the North Sea
item.description:
The British government greenlit a major offshore natural gas project in the North Sea on Wednesday, defying its own climate change pledge to halt new fossil fuel extraction.

The approval for the Jackdaw field, off the coast of Scotland, is a major victory for Britain’s oil and gas industry, unions and cities in Britain’s energy heartland, which consider the project an economic lifeline. It is also a win for President Trump, who has pressured a succession of British leaders to “open up” the North Sea to new oil and gas drilling.

Amid a sharp rise in energy prices caused by the war in Iran, British leaders cast the decision as a crucial step toward reducing the country’s reliance on imported fuels. Jackdaw’s gas would be used in Britain and fed into the gas network.

“We’re committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050,” Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said in a statement. But, he added, “Even on our ambitious climate path, we’ll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That’s why we’re taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea.”

Mr. Burnham also on Wednesday announced the creation of a government fund to support renewable energy. According to the energy ministry, the fund will begin with 2 billion pounds (about $2.6 billion) in funds with future revenue from offshore drilling feeding into it over time.

Environmental activists called the approval of Jackdaw a betrayal of the country’s efforts to transition to renewable energy. They noted that the decision comes weeks ahead of a United Nations climate summit in Turkey, where Mr. Burnham has said he will lead the British delegation and “meet the climate challenge.”

This week the United Nations reported that the world needs to cut greenhouse gas emissions — created mostly by the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas — by nearly a fifth in the next four years to avoid the most dangerous consequences of climate change.

“Jackdaw won’t make a lot of difference to our energy bills, but it will fuel the climate chaos already unfurling in front of us,” said Danny Gross, a campaigner for Friends of the Earth, an environmental group.

Mr. Burnham’s government has left an even more contentious decision — whether to allow a separate offshore oil development in the North Sea known as Rosebank — for a later date.

Jackdaw will be the first new oil and gas extraction in Britain’s North Sea since the Labour government imposed a moratorium on new drilling in 2024.

Adura, a joint venture between Shell, the British oil giant, and the Norwegian energy company Equinor, intends to develop the project. It has said work on the field could begin immediately after approval

Neil McCulloch, chief executive of Adura, urged Mr. Burnham to also approve the Rosebank project.

“Taken together, Jackdaw and Rosebank offer significant benefits for the U.K.,” Mr. McCulloch said in a statement. At their peaks, he said, the projects could provide around 10 percent of the country’s domestic gas and oil production.

Britain imports most of its oil and gas, and the war in Iran has pushed up the costs by disrupting global energy markets. Supporters of new North Sea drilling argue that expanding domestic extraction is essential to safeguarding Britain’s energy security and shielding households from price volatility.

Adura estimated that Jackdaw’s gas could meet 6 percent of Britain’s gas needs and heat 1.4 million homes, reducing the country’s reliance on imported liquefied natural gas. The field is believed to hold gas equivalent to about 200 million barrels of oil.

Supporters of new drilling argue that even as Britain transitions to clean energy, the nation will remain dependent on natural gas for decades. After all, 85 percent of Britain’s homes and businesses still use boilers for hot water and central heating, and 30 million vehicles still run on petroleum. New domestic sources will help ease Britain’s reliance on imports.

While a portion of those imports comes via pipeline from Norway — a neighbor with strict environmental regulations — the rest must be shipped across oceans as liquefied natural gas, or L.N.G. Supplying Britain from far-flung producers like Qatar, Peru, and Trinidad and Tobago carries a significantly higher carbon footprint because of the energy required to cool and transport the gas.

“Jackdaw is 99.9 percent complete and with approval now secured, gas from this field will be flowing into homes up and down the country within weeks,” Russell Borthwick, chief executive of the Aberdeen & Grampian Chamber of Commerce said in a statement.

He called the approval “a direct, tangible boost to the U.K.’s energy security at a time when it matters most.”

Environmental groups have estimated Jackdaw’s gas will serve closer to 2 percent of the country’s needs and noted that Britain would still require imports. They also maintained that new oil and gas extraction diverts money and momentum from renewable power.

“Jackdaw has been oversold,” said Tessa Khan, the executive director of Uplift, a British environmental group.

“Clean energy is how we lower bills and reindustrialize regions, not by caving to an oil industry making obscene profits while pushing up bills, laying off workers and driving the heat waves we saw this summer,” Ms. Khan said.

There is also the question of whether the approval of Jackdaw violates domestic and international commitments.

Rosebank was first approved in 2022 and Jackdaw a year later, when the Conservative Party was in power. But environmental groups sued, and those approvals were later overturned.

In 2024, nearly 200 nations agreed at a United Nations climate summit to transition away from fossil fuels. A few months later, the Labour government under Keir Starmer, who preceded Mr. Burnham, pledged a moratorium on new drilling licenses.

Mr. Burnham inherited that pledge when he became prime minister in July. But since both fields were licensed under a previous government, supporters argued, allowing exploration to move forward again does not violate the moratorium.

For the fog-shrouded stretch of the Scottish coastline around Aberdeen, the epicenter of Britain’s oil industry, the approval offers a new economic opportunity. The region has endured a quarter-century of declining North Sea production, with the local business chamber reporting losses of more than 1,000 oil and gas jobs each month.

The anxiety over the basin’s decline was underscored in August when BP announced plans to sell its North Sea business after six decades of operations there.

Oil and gas industry officials said the approval of Jackdaw was unlikely to change BP’s decision. It also won’t change the fundamental geology of the North Sea basin, where about 93 percent of oil and gas has already been extracted.

But, they argued, the project would provide enough investment to keep jobs steady as Britain sought to bolster renewable energy industries like offshore wind.

For Mr. Burnham, the decision is one of the first tests of how he will balance demands from progressive lawmakers in his party with the economic realities that face his government.

Many Labour members of Parliament are counting on Mr. Burnham to be a more robust supporter of their pro-environment agenda than Mr. Starmer was. During two decades in public life, Mr. Burnham has frequently endorsed net-zero policies and vowed to be part of the fight against climate change.

But the wars in Ukraine and Iran have driven up the price of energy and left many in the country angry about the rising cost of living.

Those goals — maintaining his party’s commitment to the environment and promising to lower energy costs — could prove difficult to achieve at the same time. Since Mr. Burnham took office, his aides have suggested he will take a “pragmatic” approach to energy, by accepting the need for dependence on fossil fuels in the short run but pushing the country toward a sustainable transition over time.

In his first call as prime minister with President Trump, Mr. Burnham also promised that he would be pragmatic about the North Sea energy fields. “There is a resource there,” the prime minister told reporters. “When people are struggling, we can’t ignore that.”

In some ways, Mr. Burnham’s decision to approve new drilling is a strange alignment with Mr. Trump, who has berated British prime ministers for embracing net-zero policies and failing to drill more in the North Sea.

Despite Mr. Trump’s vocal support for British offshore extraction, American oil giants have almost entirely abandoned the North Sea, driven out by declining yields in mature fields and higher operating costs.

ConocoPhillips sold off its British fields in 2019, followed by Exxon Mobil, which parted with decades of North Sea holdings to refocus capital on U.S. shale and South American deepwater projects. Chevron, the last major American holdout, also sold its remaining British North Sea assets.

Michael D. Shear contributed reporting from London.

item.title: For an Experiment in Political Affirmative Action, Look to Taiwan
item.description:
The United States view of Taiwan is often through the lens of a possible conflict with China or its dominance in advanced chip manufacturing. But behind the silicon shield is a vibrant democracy of 23 million people that was the first in Asia to legalize same-sex marriage and had a voter turnout of over 70 percent in its 2024 presidential election.

It has also been running one of the world’s longest experiments in political affirmative action.

For decades, Taiwan has used quotas and reserved seats to bring women into electoral politics. Today its political representation by women is among the highest in the world, and, as new research suggests, few of them were ultimately elected based on quotas.

Women hold 42 percent of Taiwan’s legislative seats, the highest share in Asia and comparable to Nordic countries. It elected its first female president in 2016 and re-elected her four years later. It has also elected two female vice presidents since 2000.

“People often argue that elections should simply be about choosing the best and most capable,” said Chang-Ling Huang, a professor at National Taiwan University who has studied gender politics for more than 20 years. Taiwan’s experience shows that “gender quotas are precisely what allow a society to truly elect the best and the most capable.”

“Otherwise,” Ms. Huang added, “patriarchal systems simply exclude qualified women from the race.”

Since the 1990s, a trend of gender quotas in elections has spread around the globe, with more than 130 countries, including more than two dozen in Europe, introducing constitutional, electoral or political party quotas for women in elections, according to data from the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance, an intergovernmental organization.

But Taiwan’s approach began much earlier. In 1946, the Republic of China passed a Constitution that reserved seats for women in elections, a result of a women’s movement that dated back to the 1920s and the influence of socialism in the country, said Ms. Huang, the political scientist. When the Nationalist government was defeated in the civil war and moved to Taiwan in 1949, the quotas, set at 5 to 10 percent, were followed in local elections even though the Constitution was largely suspended during the next decades of authoritarian rule.

As Taiwan began to democratize in 1987, some feminist organizations worried that quotas could send a message that women were incapable of winning elections on their own merits. But they ultimately decided to lean into quotas. They fought for and succeeded in getting four rounds of major quota reforms over the next few decades.

A law that took effect in 2002 guarantees women a seat in local council districts electing four or more members. If, say, four men received the highest numbers of votes for a four-person council, the fourth seat would go to the female candidate with the most votes, regardless of party affiliations. So the law created an incentive for all political parties to recruit and nominate female candidates. In 2030, the quota will go up to one in three, and will be gender neutral. It means that in every three seats there must be at least one woman and one man.

After studying data sets from six election cycles from 2002 to 2022, Ms. Huang found that female candidates became very competitive over time. The number of electoral districts that needed to activate a reserved seat dropped from 31 in 2002 to just four in 2022.

Now women rarely need reserved seats to get elected, but the existence of those seats remains crucial to securing party nominations. “They serve as a safeguard, even when they go unused,” Ms. Huang said.

What if Taiwan had never adopted gender quotas? A redo of history isn’t possible, of course, but Japan provides a fairly good comparison. Women in both Japan and the Republic of China won their suffrage right after the World War II. And Taiwan’s election system resembles Japan’s. But Japan never reserved seats for women, and today women hold only 15 percent of seats in Parliament. (Women make up 28 percent of the U.S. Congress, which puts the country 84th in a global ranking of the percentage of women in national legislatures.)

Women make up about a quarter of China’s Parliament, a percentage that has barely moved since 1970s. In Xi Jinping’s third term as China’s leader, there’s not a single woman in the Communist Party’s Politburo, breaking a tradition of more than two decades. In the party’s 77 years ruling the country, no woman has ever been appointed to the Standing Committee, the pinnacle of C.C.P. power. The government under Mr. Xi has systematically tightened restrictions on feminist advocacy and movements like #MeToo.

The biggest impact of the quota system in Taiwan is that it made women in political office ordinary rather than extraordinary, Ms. Huang said.

With Taiwan gearing up for local elections in late November, giant campaign posters of female candidates seem to be everywhere on the island, especially in big cities.

Su Chiao-hui is running as the mayoral candidate of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party in New Taipei City, a metropolitan ring of more than four million residents that surrounds the capital city, Taipei, and is a stronghold of the opposition Nationalist Party (K.M.T.).

It’s a high-stakes election, and Ms. Su, 50, a three-term legislator representing a district in the city, is running against Lee Shu-chuan, a 68-year-old political veteran whose English name is Hammer.

Ms. Su’s party emphasizes Taiwan’s distinct identity while Mr. Lee’s party has historically tied its identity in the Republic of China that was founded in mainland in 1912. But in this local race, campaigns are intensely personal and practical. Candidates meet voters face to face and make their case on housing, child care, transportation and other everyday issues.

Ms. Su’s campaign embraces a feminine, maternal image — she hosts a children’s storytelling podcast — suggesting that she is comfortable with that side of herself and believes voters are, too.

Her campaign office has a vibe of a children’s activity room, with pastel blocks, oversize pink lettering and cheerful cartoon figures of “Otter Mom,” her podcast. She hopes the persona projects an approachable, family-friendly image targeted at younger voters and parents who value education.

The rising women’s representation in electoral politics has not erased gender stereotypes and misogyny in Taiwan.

Yu-Yu Liu, an activist turned township head in central rural Taiwan, said that when she first ran for the office four years ago, many voters told her that, at 35, she was too young. Then almost in the same breath they would comment that she needed to hurry up to get married. She sometimes felt subtly isolated at traditional political networking gatherings where older men drank and smoked.

Even Tsai Ing-wen, Taiwan’s first female president, endured many misogynistic attacks. An opponent called her an ill-fated woman. She was questioned over her qualifications to understand parental issues because she’s a single, childless woman (who raised two cats and five dogs during her presidency). After her party suffered a huge defeat in the 2018 local elections, some people questioned whether she would be a one-term president.

“I told myself,” she said in a recent meeting at her office, “as the first female president, I can’t fail.” She was re-elected two years later.

item.title: A Battle for Control of India’s Biggest Business Empire
item.description:
Who actually controls India’s biggest company?

A bitter power struggle over the Tata Group, a 158-year-old conglomerate with more than a million employees worldwide and $180 billion in annual revenue, has become a test of who calls the shots in Indian capitalism: owners, professional managers or the government.

The fight pits the family-led charitable trusts that own two-thirds of Tata Sons, the group’s holding company, against the powerful chairman who runs its businesses. India’s government has emerged as a wild card, pressing Tata Sons to list on the stock market — a move that could permanently reshape its ownership and weaken the founding family’s control.

The conflict simmered for at least a year before bursting into the open. In August, Natarajan Chandrasekaran, one of India’s most celebrated chief executives, stunned the business world by announcing he would not seek another five-year term as chairman. He cited opposition from one board member to his staying beyond February.

That “absence of unanimous support” would hurt the company when “many strategic projects” are under “critical stages of execution,” he wrote in a letter at the time. “Clarity on leadership is important for employees, investors, partners and other stakeholders.”

A month later, he reversed course. At a Sept. 17 meeting, a majority of the board voted to reappoint him. Noel Tata, a board member and head of the Tata Trusts, a group of public charities that owns 66 percent of Tata Sons, had cast the sole dissenting vote.

Mr. Tata called the vote to reappoint Mr. Chandrasekaran “illegal” because it had bypassed his veto. Later that day, he wrote that Mr. Chandrasekaran had “freely” chosen to resign and that it was time to “turn the page.” Since then, his office has filed dozens of legal motions preparing to challenge the vote.

The dispute could reverberate across Indian businesses, where founding families retain control of many of the largest companies, even when professional managers run the day-to-day operations.

Amit Tandon, founder of the Mumbai-based Institutional Investor Advisory Services, said he could not recall any other board mutiny against a controlling shareholder in India. About two-thirds of the country’s biggest companies are family-owned, he said.

“Business families will see the dispute as a warning that ownership alone does not guarantee control,” he said.

India’s business dynasties don’t want their hired managers wresting control of companies that families spent generations building. Mr. Chandrasekaran’s supporters see a different threat. They argue that the Tata Group is too important to India to be governed by antiquated ownership arrangements or the whims of a founding family.

Vijay Singh, a former secretary of defense who served on the Tata Sons board and remains a trustee of some of the seven charities that own it, draws a clear distinction between ownership and management.

The trustees “may be owners, but they’re not entitled to run the companies,” said Mr. Singh, who supports Mr. Chandrasekaran. “The charities and the business were meant to be unconnected.”

The stakes for this boardroom battle are enormous because Tata is woven into almost every facet of Indian life.

Arrive in Mumbai on a Tata-owned airline and you can ride in a Tata-made taxi to a Tata hotel, passing billboards for Tata real estate or Tata life insurance along the way. The tea in your room may be Tata’s. So might your watch or jewelry. If you are reading this on a new iPhone, there is a good chance that it was assembled in India by Tata.

Few countries have a corporate institution quite like it. Tata is trusted, even loved, not just for its products but for its philanthropy. The Tata Trusts support cancer hospitals, scientific research, nutrition programs and the performing arts. Some of the charities predate India’s independence.

Now the two pillars of Tata — its businesses and its charities — are at war.

From offices high in Mumbai’s World Trade Center, Noel Tata, a descendant of the founder, Jamsetji Tata, presides over the trusts. They own two-thirds of Tata Sons, which holds substantial stakes in the group companies listed on stock exchanges, as well as its private businesses and real estate, and controls the corporate brand.

A mile and a half away, Mr. Chandrasekaran and his management team run the empire from Bombay House, the elegant headquarters built in 1924 and renovated after he took over in 2017. There, in fourth-floor boardrooms, his allies organize their defense against what they see as Mr. Tata’s overbearing interference.

The legal entanglement reflects a conglomerate with a complicated history stretching back to the 19th century. But this is more than a feud between two men. At the center of the struggle is a government push to force Tata Sons onto the stock market, turning a governance dispute into an existential fight over ownership.

In 2022, the Reserve Bank of India introduced rules that threatened to force Tata Sons to list on the stock market. Going public would require the holding company to sell 25 percent of its equity to outside investors, diluting existing shareholders.

The central bank’s rationale was India’s financial stability. Regulators argued that Tata Sons was so deeply enmeshed in the country’s financial system that its debt could have made it “too big to fail” — meaning its collapse might threaten the banking system. They said wider ownership and disclosure requirements for public companies would reduce the risk.

Initially, both Mr. Tata and Mr. Chandrasekaran opposed a forced listing. In 2024, the group paid off all of its debt, hoping to satisfy the regulator’s demands without surrendering its private status.

But this June, the central bank said debt levels were irrelevant. Any organization with assets exceeding a trillion rupees, or about $10.3 billion, the bank declared, had to be listed, a threshold well below Tata Sons’ size.

Forcing a private company to sell shares to the public as protection against a hypothetical financial crisis would be an extraordinary intervention, with few comparable precedents.

By the Sept. 17 meeting, with most of the board behind him, Mr. Chandrasekaran decided Tata Sons should list. Management and the government were now aligned. Noel Tata and the trusts were determined to keep it private.

The government’s role went beyond financial regulation.

Since May, the Maharashtra Charity Commissioner, a little-known official under a state government run by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s political party, has blocked Mr. Tata from convening one of the trusts. That has stopped him from calling a shareholder vote to remove Mr. Chandrasekaran and fight to keep Tata Sons private. The commissioner has been responding to complaints filed by some trustees, including Mr. Singh, who have filed motions challenging Mr. Tata’s control of the trusts.

Mr. Chandrasekaran is an attractive ally for the government. He rose through Tata Consultancy Services, the conglomerate’s technology services arm. Since he became chairman nine years ago, the combined market capitalization of Tata’s 26 listed subsidiaries has more than doubled to about $300 billion.

But some of his boldest investments have been expensive and unprofitable. In 2022, Tata bought Air India from the government, which had nationalized it from Tata nearly seven decades earlier. The group is also undertaking a $12 billion semiconductor manufacturing project in India — a long shot that could take more than a decade to pay off, even in the best of circumstances.

Financing these ambitions can be tricky. Tata Sons has reduced its borrowing, while Tata Consultancy Services, the group’s cash engine, faces growing pressure as artificial intelligence reshapes the technology industry. Listing Tata Sons could raise capital for these long-term commitments.

Nirmalya Kumar, a former Tata Group strategy chief who worked with both Noel Tata and Mr. Chandrasekaran and is now a visiting professor at the Indian School of Business in Hyderabad, sees an uncomfortable convergence of corporate ambitions and political priorities.

Mr. Kumar, who was fired 10 years ago during a boardroom clash that forced out a previous chairman of Tata Sons, said he believed Mr. Modi and Mr. Chandrasekaran enjoyed a “symbiotic relationship,” pursuing showy projects with “the house money” generated by Tata’s established businesses.

Yet Mr. Kumar also thinks Tata’s ownership structure has outlived its usefulness.

A company of that size, he said, should “be public so that it can get scrutiny and is not being done on the whim of one person.”

item.title: Senator Asks 4 Accounting Giants to Describe Malta Tax Advice
item.description:
Senator Ron Wyden, the ranking Democrat of the Senate Finance Committee, on Tuesday requested detailed information on how the four biggest accounting firms use Malta to help multinational companies based in the United States dodge billions of dollars in taxes.

The New York Times reported in August that big companies are setting up subsidiaries in Malta, often in empty offices, to shield their profits from taxes around the world. Companies including Crocs, Victoria’s Secret, Abbott Laboratories and Thermo Fisher have used the tiny archipelago to exploit its near-zero effective corporate tax rate, shifting taxable profits away from countries where they have actual employees and customers.

The Big Four accounting firms — KPMG, Deloitte, EY and PwC — have advised companies on the arrangements, engineering schemes to cut their clients’ tax bills by navigating the differences in tax laws of various countries.

KPMG declined to comment. Deloitte, EY and PwC did not respond to requests for comment.

“While working-class Americans dutifully pay taxes on every paycheck, sophisticated accountants and tax lawyers are devising clever strategies for corporate giants to continue exploiting offshore tax havens to avoid paying their fair share,” Mr. Wyden, of Oregon, wrote in a letter to each of the firms.

The letter requested descriptions of the firms’ Malta strategies, along with copies of “presentations, slide decks or other marketing materials” for corporate tax strategies using Malta. It also asked for documents specifying how much companies saved in taxes, as well as details of fees for devising or marketing such tax strategies and the number of clients that have used them.

Malta, the smallest country in the European Union, said in 2023 that it would delay until 2029 a minimum corporate income tax that dozens of countries had adopted as part of an international crackdown. President Trump withdrew the United States from the enforcement effort on his first day back in office, boosting Malta’s appeal as a tax haven.

The number of Maltese subsidiaries set up by U.S. companies has risen about 70 percent over the past three years, public records show.

item.title: SpaceX and Tesla Explore Merger to Create a De Facto Elon Inc.
item.description:
Elon Musk has taken a big step toward creating Elon Inc.

The world’s richest person said on Tuesday that SpaceX and Tesla were exploring a merger, which would consolidate his interests in rockets, electric cars and artificial intelligence into a multitrillion-dollar behemoth.

Mr. Musk is both the chief executive and the largest shareholder of both companies. During an earnings call for SpaceX, he said that the boards of the rocket maker and the electric car manufacturer had formed special committees of independent directors to consider a merger.

“Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes,” he said. But as a conflicted party, who could essentially decide the terms of the deal, he said he would not be in on the discussions, he added.

Mr. Musk’s statements were the clearest sign that he is exploring whether to create a technology giant that could be worth some $3.5 trillion given the companies’s current market values. Since SpaceX held its initial public offering in June, its executives have publicly flirted with the idea of combining Mr. Musk’s two crown jewels.

The idea of a merger has garnered support not only from Mr. Musk, but also his legions of fans and investors, who see synergies in software development and hardware manufacturing between SpaceX, which encompasses rockets, A.I. models and the Starlink satellite internet service, and Tesla, which makes cars, self-driving technology and robots.

But a consolidation of Mr. Musk’s business empire has also raised concerns from some lawmakers and critics, who believe that the world’s richest person, whose net worth has recently hovered around $1 trillion, has already amassed too much power.

Mr. Musk, Tesla and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment.

SpaceX’s stock jumped 8 percent in premarket trading on Wednesday, while Tesla’s gained about 1 percent.

Tesla reports its latest quarterly earnings on Wednesday, after the close of trading in U.S. markets. Mr. Musk will probably face more questions about the possible merger on a call with analysts.

Beyond sharing a chief executive, Tesla and SpaceX have deep connections. Mr. Musk has moved money and workers between companies, and the carmaker has sold hundreds of millions of dollars in batteries and vehicles to the rocket maker, according to financial filings. Tesla invested in xAI, the A.I. company that merged with SpaceX earlier this year, and Tesla and SpaceX plan to produce A.I. chips together at a joint factory called Terafab.

Micah Walter-Range, an analyst for VettaFi Space Index, a stock index that tracks commercial space companies, called a merger between SpaceX and Tesla “an intriguing concept.”

“It’s not hard to see why a vertically integrated company seems attractive,” he said. “Tesla robots linked by Starlink to xAI data centers for control and A.I. model training purposes would give SpaceX an end-to-end advantage that nobody else could replicate quickly.”

Last week, during a launch event for Tesla’s new Roadster, Mr. Musk looked on as a vehicle deployed thrusters under its chassis that lifted the car over a row of other Tesla vehicles, including a Semi truck. The car did a flip as it passed overhead.

Musk said that SpaceX engineers had worked on the Tesla product. The demonstration showed “what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world best rocket company,” he noted.

For months, Mr. Musk and his executives have hinted at the idea of a merger. When SpaceX went public in June, its president and chief operating officer, Gwynne Shotwell, told CNBC that “there’s no question that there are synergies between Tesla and SpaceX in our futures.” She also said that a deal between SpaceX and Tesla “might make Elon’s life a little easier.”

Last month, when asked about the possibility of a tie-up onstage at a technology conference in Los Angeles, Mr. Musk said: “Who can imagine what action one might take when there’s so much close collaboration.”

Mr. Musk wields an enormous amount of power and influence at both companies. He controls roughly 20 percent of shareholder votes at Tesla and more than 80 percent of votes at SpaceX. A merger would give Mr. Musk much greater control over Tesla, which he has long sought. In 2024, he demanded that Tesla give him 25 percent of the company if it wanted him to keep working on products based on A.I.

The boards of both companies are stacked with his allies, including the directors considered independent for corporate governance purposes. The boards feature longtime investors, a family member and friends, some of whom have vacationed with Mr. Musk. Ira Ehrenpreis, an investor who has been close to Mr. Musk for years, is an independent director at both Tesla and SpaceX.

Tesla’s chairwoman, Robyn Denholm, vigorously campaigned last year for a pay package of more than $1 trillion for Mr. Musk that was approved by shareholders. The compensation was justified because he made achievements “that no one else has done before, doing things that further humankind, that have an impact on the world,” she told The New York Times last year.

On Tuesday, Mr. Musk said that the special committees considering a merger were formed “at the request of shareholders,” but did not clarify when or how those requests were made. Corporate law in Texas, where Tesla and SpaceX have their corporate domiciles, makes it difficult for aggrieved investors to challenge management decisions.

He said that agreement on a deal by Tesla would require 50 percent of all shareholder votes. Although not directly involved in the merger talks, he later noted that the committees had not yet “reached an agreement on the terms of any transaction and there’s no guarantee that they will.”

But, he added, “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies.”

Recently, Mr. Musk has used his X account, which has more than 241 million followers, to rally fans and investors into voting for his favored company initiatives. Ahead of the vote for his latest Tesla pay package, both he and the company used their accounts on the social platform, now owned by SpaceX, to encourage shareholders to approve the plan.

The potential mega-merger would cap an incredible 12 months of personal deal-making by Mr. Musk, who earlier this year merged his A.I. company, xAI, with SpaceX, before taking that combined entity public in June. His net worth has skyrocketed, and he has become by far the biggest known political donor ahead of November’s midterm elections, spending more than $276 million to support Republican groups.

If Democrats retake either house of Congress, however, there may be greater scrutiny over Mr. Musk’s companies, said Ross Gerber, the chief executive of Gerber Kawasaki, an investment firm that owns SpaceX stock. The investor noted that Mr. Musk has a small window in which to complete a deal.

“The longer he waits, the less time he has,” Mr. Gerber said.

Kate Conger contributed reporting.

item.title: SpaceX Boosts the A.I. Rally
item.description:
Andrew here. We’ve got all of the news about a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger below, but let’s get into the report everyone is talking about: Did Elon Musk throttle Ukraine’s access to the Starshield service run by Starlink, as The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday? Or did the Trump administration?

When Ukraine made the accusation last week, Musk seemingly suggested that any such decision was made by the White House: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” he wrote on social media. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”

That was repeatedly quoted, but the post also said: “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”

What Musk is effectively saying is that any customer — including Ukraine — using Starlink for offensive military purposes could have its access restricted. In war, it’s often unclear where defense ends and offense begins. (That said, Starshield, which Ukraine has been using, is meant for military uses.)

Secretary of State Marco Rubio echoed this argument on Wednesday. Starlink, he said: is “not a military system, although it could be used in order to guide drones and things of this nature and so forth. And then Starshield is different. It’s a unique defense product that is sold and operated through the Department of War, as an example. It’s two different items and it’s important to distinguish one from the other.”

Of course, this raises a broader question: Should a single private citizen wield such disproportionate geopolitical leverage? Right now, there is no competition for this service. I’ll be speaking with Musk next month at the DealBook Summit. In the meantime, watch this space: If Democrats take the House, and possibly the Senate, expect lots of hearings on this topic.

Investors in SpaceX got a lot of what they were looking for in the company’s quarterly results on Tuesday, and then some.

Elon Musk confirmed that the boards of both the rocket and artificial intelligence company and Tesla had formed special committees to study a potential union.

Just as important: SpaceX disclosed better-than-expected results from its increasingly expensive A.I. business — even as it further underscored how much of corporate America’s future is riding on the A.I. boom.

Could a SpaceX-Tesla deal happen? Many on Wall Street have long anticipated that Musk will pursue one. The formation of the special committees is a tangible step toward that.

But Musk cautioned that while he thinks it’s a good idea, saying it will happen “would be overstating it.” He added that any such proposal would require approval from at least 50 percent of all outstanding shares in Tesla. That, he said, is “quite a high hurdle to achieve.”

Musk owns about 44 percent of shares in SpaceX and 28 percent of shares in Tesla.

It’s largely about A.I. Both companies are developing various aspects of the technology, and analysts see some merit in meshing that work.

SpaceX showed investors a glimpse of A.I.’s business potential. The company swung to a $4.4 billion profit for the quarter from a loss a year ago, while revenue more than doubled from a year earlier to $14.5 billion. A big reason: soaring revenue from leasing cloud computing to other A.I. companies like Anthropic, which tripled quarter on quarter to $7.6 billion.

“We could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone,” Musk told analysts.

But SpaceX is also spending heavily, with capital expenditures hitting $19.6 billion in the quarter, nearly tripling year on year. That increasingly ties the future of SpaceX — and that of many others — to hopes that the A.I. boom will continue.

Ken Griffin became the latest A.I. spending spree skeptic, saying at a conference on Tuesday that markets were “almost certainly” in a bubble. The billionaire financier also questioned how much utility corporate America was actually getting from its huge spending on the technology.

Investors appear unfazed for now. Shares in SpaceX are up in premarket trading. That could be a comfort for Anthropic, which is expected to stage its I.P.O. as soon as next month, and for OpenAI, which is reportedly raising money again.

Middle East oil flows surpass prewar levels. Shipments averaged more than 24 million barrels a day in the week through Oct. 18 — roughly 700,000 barrels above the average level before the start of the war in Iran — The Wall Street Journal reports, citing data from the maritime analysis firm Kpler. But rising shipping costs and disruptions at oil refineries are expected to keep pressure on fuel prices. Brent, the global benchmark for oil, was trading above $109 a barrel on Wednesday.

OpenAI’s artificial intelligence agents go rogue again. This time, they targeted an internal monitoring system intended to flag the misbehavior of artificial intelligence models, Bloomberg reported. OpenAI and others have faced issues with runaway technology. Now, OpenAI said it was studying whether its agents had a broader tendency to try to escape monitoring.

President Trump vows to spend heavily on the midterms. The president said he would spend an additional $100 million on Republican candidates by Election Day, on top of the $300 million he said his political machine had already spent, as some polls suggested the party was trailing. Separately, Mike Bloomberg’s team said he was giving about $80 million to help Democratic candidates.

The big question hanging over earnings season is whether climbing interest rates and energy costs will dent corporate profits. A roundup of Tuesday’s quarterly results — excluding SpaceX — show the challenges boardrooms face.

Here are a few:

G.M.: The carmaker’s stock price has flagged this year amid the Trump administration’s trade war and elevated fuel prices. In response, the company announced a $20 billion stock buyback plan. But investors were more focused on G.M.’s downbeat earnings forecast, sending shares lower.

United Airlines: The carrier’s revenue and earnings fell short of analysts’ expectations and were hurt by higher fuel prices. United sees more turbulence ahead, forecasting that fuel prices will rise to an average of $4.80 a gallon this quarter, from an average of $3.90 in the previous quarter.

Netflix: The streaming giant, which last week announced layoffs and a big management shake-up, reported its slowest rate of quarterly revenue percentage growth in three years. (Its $3.66 billion net income beat Wall Street expectations.) Netflix is struggling with viewership, and offered lackluster guidance for this quarter; Ted Sarandos, one of its C.E.O.s, said that “we could do better.”

Up next: Investors will pay attention to what other bellwethers — including Procter & Gamble on Thursday and American Express on Friday — say about consumer spending and the economy.

The race to feed the law industry’s growing appetite for artificial intelligence tools is intensifying. A.I. giants are introducing products catered to lawyers while venture capital funnels near record amounts of cash into legal tech.

Few companies are ramping up resources faster than Legora, a legal services provider. On Wednesday, it is announcing a $550 million round of funding at an $8.8 billion valuation, Sarah Kessler is first to report. That’s up from a $5.55 billion valuation in March.

Legora has about $200 million in annual recurring revenue. In March, the metric stood at about $100 million, according to the company. Max Junestrand, Legora’s C.E.O., told DealBook that his number of employees had grown to 1,000 from 200 since the beginning of the year.

The U.S. is now Legora’s largest market by sales. The Stockholm-based software maker opened its first U.S. office last year and counts about half of the largest 50 law firms as customers.

Harvey, its biggest U.S. competitor, raised $550 million at a $15.5 billion valuation in September and has an annual recurring revenue of more than $400 million.

Atreides Management led Legora’s round. New participants included Fidelity Management & Research Company and JPMorgan Chase.

“Legal is a sophisticated market with demanding buyers, and the bar for software is high,” said Gavin Baker, the managing partner of Atreides.

The legal tech landscape is shifting: A handful of law firms, including the giant Kirkland & Ellis, have said they will build their own A.I. systems. And the personal injury firm Morgan & Morgan took it a step further with plans to sell its legal A.I. to other firms.

But Junestrand said firms with in-house A.I. tools continued to buy tech, too. “In the same way that Legora is not a law firm, very few of those organizations are really software companies,” he told DealBook.

A bigger threat could come from A.I. companies themselves. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have all released tools for lawyers this year.

Legal tech start-ups like Legora — themselves customers of the A.I. giants — have a head start in an industry that is not exactly known for its quick adoption of new technologies. Will that be enough to win?

Silicon Valley is teeming with start-ups focused on artificial intelligence and other capital-intensive businesses. That has created an appetite for more financing, and lenders like Erebor are seeking to fill it.

Erebor, which focuses on tech start-ups, will announce on Wednesday that it has secured a $30 million investment from Robinhood, the online trading platform, Niko Gallogly is first to report.

Erebor’s story: It was co-founded by Palmer Luckey, the entrepreneur and a founder of Anduril, the A.I. military start-up. After the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023, Luckey and his co-founders set out to enter the market with a bank that “deeply understands” the balance sheets of capital-intensive start-ups, Jacob Hirshman, Erebor’s chairman and co-founder, told DealBook.

Some of Erebor’s largest investors are Valor Equity Partners, Lux Capital and 8VC.

Robinhood’s investment comes out of its Robinhood Ventures Fund II, which lets ordinary investors buy into privately held start-ups.

Rapid growth: The company became the first new bank to receive a national charter during the second Trump administration. Since it opened for business in February, Erebor — named for a mountain stronghold in J.R.R. Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” — has amassed more than $7 billion in deposits.

Start-ups want more options. Young tech companies typically raise equity from venture capital firms. But that model is expensive for businesses that own or build assets.

For some tech start-ups, borrowing makes sense to avoid diluting their equity, Hirshman said. One instance: Valar Atomics.

More funding on the way: The investment comes as Erebor is closing in on a $1.5 billion fund-raising round that is expected to value the lender at about $8 billion, according to a person familiar with the deal who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak about it publicly.

It faces plenty of competition. Other firms are focusing on start-ups, including Mercury and Cross River. Other established lenders like JPMorgan Chase are also moving into the space.

Deals

Larry Ellison is said to have potentially borrowed billions more against his stock holdings, California regulatory filings show, partly to help finance his son’s takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery. (WSJ)

Salesforce agreed to buy Braze, a marketing platform, for about $5.7 billion as it races to add more artificial intelligence features to its offerings. (Bloomberg)

Politics, policy and regulation

Joel Kaplan, Meta’s global policy chief known for his Republican ties, is stepping down. (NYT)

How a proposed tax on California billionaires became a political awakening for Sergey Brin, a founder of Google. (Politico)

Best of the rest

Running a popular restaurant is hard. But many customers don’t want private equity to help. (NYT)

“Nurses Are in High Demand — but They’re Quitting in Droves” (WSJ)

We’d like your feedback! Please email thoughts and suggestions to dealbook@nytimes.com.

item.title: How We Draw Lines in a World Awash in A.I. Images
item.description:
The internet is awash in A.I.-generated video and images — think President Trump appearing to tame a tiger or unbelievable fitness transformations.

But it’s rare for The New York Times to report on specific pieces of A.I. slop, even on days when a viral clip seems to be all anyone is talking about. Why is that? How do we decide to report on certain images? And how do we know where to draw the line?

For answers, we turned to three colleagues who seek clarity in a bewildering media world: Stuart A. Thompson, who reports on online influence; Aisha Khan, the deputy Standards editor; and Mark Scheffler, who leads the Visual Investigations team.

These are edited excerpts from our conversation.

How do we decide when A.I. images and memes are newsworthy?

STUART THOMPSON: This is a tricky question! It’s one we’ve been debating since long before A.I. came along. Remember QAnon? It was this massive online conspiracy theory, but there was a lot of debate about when, why and how mainstream media should weigh in.

My golden rule is that readers need to benefit from learning about it in some way. We don’t usually just debunk. We try to explain — usually focused on the causes and consequences. Who made it, why and how do they benefit? Who is harmed? The article needs to reflect something deeper about society, technology or regulations, I think. But it’s rarely obvious when to dive in.

AISHA KHAN: As Stuart says, figuring out when to report on these can be tricky. Is it the president, or a major political candidate, sharing an A.I.-generated video or image of himself or a rival to make a political point? Are film studios turning to A.I., or are propaganda operations churning out A.I. content? What about those strange videos on YouTube Kids? Those are things we’d want to and have covered. But we also want to help our audience understand how the technology is evolving, and how to spot when someone is using A.I. to try to influence them or to sell them something.

MARK SCHEFFLER: We typically jump in when the imagery is purporting to show an incident or event with high stakes. A bombing of a building, someone appearing to perpetrate violence, attempts to deceive as part of a scam of some kind, whether it’s hawking a dubious product or trying to influence minors or other vulnerable populations. If there’s an accountability dimension, that’s when, from our perspective, it’s important for our team to cover it.

We’ve reported on how A.I. imagery is changing elections like the Los Angeles mayoral race and global affairs like the Iran war. Where’s the line between showing our audience what we’re talking about and amplifying misinformation or disinformation?

AISHA: This is a really difficult question, and one we wrestle with nearly every day. So much misinformation and disinformation is visual, now that it is easy to pump out A.I.-generated content. We don’t want to contribute to the circulation of dubious content created to mislead and sow confusion. So we take steps to choose clips and images with great care and restraint, limit what we show, and also label and mark content that is false. We also put a lot of effort into explaining and contextualizing anything we do show. And in some cases, we may decide it is better to explain the content rather than show it, for example if it is very offensive.

STUART: I prefer showing readers the content as much as possible, except for content that is vulgar or deeply offensive. The imagery and videos I see on social media are sometimes shocking, and we risk sanitizing the reality of what people are doing with A.I. tools if we write about it only obliquely. Once you see it, you understand how far things have gone. But that leads to some tough conversations inside the newsroom, since we’re also wary of amplifying something false or doing a liar’s work for them by spreading the message further.

A politician publishing an A.I. fake would have been unthinkable a few years ago. Now there are hundreds of ads floating around the midterms that are A.I.-made. We probably need to find some broader significance to an A.I. fake to consider reporting on it. There was an A.I.-generated photo of President Trump seemingly embracing an aide on a golf course. It was nothing spectacular as far as A.I. fakes go, but people started to share it as though it was real. It fed into larger speculation among critics about the aide’s relationship to Mr. Trump. It was also apparently manipulated to remove the invisible watermarks that companies insert to identify A.I. imagery. So those methods, and the power of that particular image to fit within existing narratives, were all worthy of an article.

MARK: The world is becoming awash in this material, and it’s getting more and more sophisticated. We are in a situation where objective reality is constantly being put into question and in some cases, wholly undermined. It’s important that we stay vigilant for synthetic content in our own reporting, but also continue to help people understand what it looks like and how it’s getting better and better at mimicking real-world scenes, locations, actions and people. Stuart’s work in this space is invaluable.

How do our considerations change when a world leader like President Trump posts an A.I. video?

AISHA: The president posts a lot of videos, and not all are newsworthy. But he is the head of government, and some of his posts are definitely important to cover: when they are part of a campaign or promoting a policy platform, or might be misleading on an important issue. Our readers rely on us to report on these in a straightforward and responsible way, and to make it clear why they are newsworthy and to include any information they need to understand them.

MARK: To Aisha’s point, some of these posts have more serious consequences than others, but Mr. Trump has put A.I. slop into the public discourse at the highest levels now, and we should be persistent in calling out what it is, what it might reveal and what the downstream ramifications could be.

STUART: He’s the leader of the free world. What he is doing matters. We also risk becoming desensitized to his behavior. In some ways we already are. The first A.I.-generated video he posted was national news. Now people barely blink.

A.I. videos generated for propaganda purposes may be outrageous, but many are clearly fake to a reasonable viewer — think Trump bombing protesters with excrement. How do our decisions about covering that type of video differ from reporting on deepfakes?

STUART: At the beginning of this new A.I. age, watchdogs worried that A.I. deepfakes would flood the internet. What we got instead were a lot of memes, and relatively fewer deceptive deepfakes. But memes still have a lot of power. It’s less about debunking them than understanding what they’re being used for, and why.

MARK: I agree with Stuart that things that are more reflections of what people want to believe — whether they’re ludicrously presented or obviously fake — can still get a lot of traction. With the more sophisticated efforts to deceive, you start to add motive or suspected motive to the mix. Why is this person or entity doing this? Do they have an active stake in an outcome? That’s harder to determine and report out, but it’s key.

Are there best practices for displaying manipulated images that make news?

AISHA: We have come up with a system for how we show A.I. videos. We try to label any such content with a prominent “Generated by A.I.” label. When the videos or photos feature false or misleading content, we also overlay a red slash on them to make it clear these are disinformation.

It sounds like all this work takes time. How do we build that in while still being fast to a story?

MARK: Everyone at The Times works in a highly competitive news world. That’s a given. On Visual Investigations, we abide by the longstanding adage that it’s better to be right than to be first. It’s nice when you can be both obviously. But if things aren’t adding up, we keep reporting and trying to shore up the facts.

Have we ever gone too far, or not far enough, in showing manipulated imagery?

STUART: There was a lot of debate about my most recent piece about A.I. in campaign advertising. In the original draft, we included the full clips of the ads with sound, which included some extreme imagery. One ad showed caricatures of what appeared to be Iranian leaders, invited to a party with a candidate where they used scimitars to stab at a cake featuring the Star of David. I can describe it here, but seeing it is something else entirely. It was weird and disturbing. Is that worth showing to readers? I think it’s good if the public really grasps how far politicians and candidates are going with A.I., and what these systems are capable of producing. We decided to omit that clip, and described it in text instead.

AISHA: As Stuart notes, we have lively discussions about how much or little to show. In the case of A.I. in campaign ads, we wanted to show how quickly and well it can be used to create both over-the-top caricatures and very realistic ads, but without posting some of the most offensive content or giving these operations the visibility they seek.

Are we ever 100 percent certain that an outside photo or video isn’t A.I.-generated? If so, will there be a time when that will cease to be the case?

MARK: We are having to add steps to our verification and corroboration process. It’s not just a question of when and where something happened, it’s also: Did it happen at all? That requires all of our usual checks and balances, everything from doing sun/shadow calculations to tracking down the provenance of a piece of footage. And now we’re bringing increased scrutiny to our assessment of footage, looking for visual anomalies or inconsistencies with time and place, digging deeper into the metadata of a video clip and redoubling our efforts to understand when and where the footage first appeared online.

Most of the material we work with includes fragments of footage, filmed at odd angles, often at night, with low resolution, etc., so potentially easier to fake. I think with the robust corroboration methods we use, we decrease the possibility of getting duped, but we never cut corners and always try to anticipate new developments. It’s hard to know what the future will unspool.

item.title: Alaska’s Journalists Join Forces to Cover the Midterms
item.description:
Like her peers in the news business, Claire Stremple, editor in chief of The Alaska Beacon, writes regular memos detailing which stories are in the pipeline, who’s working on them and when they’re likely to be published.

Then she does something that those peers generally don’t do: She sends that memo to the Beacon’s competitors.

Dozens of news organizations in Alaska have drifted from conventional notions of media rivalry to an all-terrain embrace of collaboration on stories large and small. Driven by scarce resources and the geographic realities of a state bigger than California, Texas and Montana combined, they are republishing one another’s stories, and even collaborating across newsrooms on voter guides and other articles.

Veteran journalists in the state have come to view competing outlets working on the same story as wasteful duplication. “There are so many stories in Alaska and so much here that goes uncovered, and there is absolutely no good reason why anyone should be competing at this point,” said Nathaniel Herz, executive editor of The Anchorage Press, a monthly newspaper. “Resources now are such that it really does cry out for better cooperation.”

This collaboration has become central to the coverage of one of the nation’s most scrutinized midterm races. Former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat, is challenging Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, in a tight race that could help determine control of the Senate. The campaign features a quirk that invites far-flung coverage: Another candidate on the ballot shares the same first and last names of Senator Sullivan, prompting complaints from Republicans, including President Trump, that “Decoy Dan” is out to rig the election by siphoning votes. Both Mr. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have recently made campaign stops in the state to barnstorm for Senator Sullivan.

The constraints have propelled efforts to spread the existing coverage as broadly as possible. The nonprofit Alaska News Coalition this year started a platform on which about eight newspapers have been exchanging content, according to Larry Persily, the organization’s executive director. And The Alaska Beacon, part of the States Newsroom nonprofit, which has a philanthropic business model that stresses sharing of content and story planning, this year saw its stories republished nearly 3,000 times by other outlets through the end of August.

But article-sharing in Alaska is commonly an informal and ad hoc phenomenon. “We pretty much always say yes” to republication requests, said Vicky Ho, the top editor of The Anchorage Daily News.

Kyle Hopkins, the lead reporter in a collaboration of The Anchorage Daily News and ProPublica that earned the 2020 Pulitzer Prize for public service, said that when he learns that another journalist is working on the same story, he’ll reach out to propose a joint effort, “rather than rushing to beat each other.”

Alaska’s public media outlets, a critical news lifeline for hard-to-reach communities, are also scouring the horizon for partnerships.

“In years past, our network was similar to any other news organizations, where we’d be working on other stories and seeing whether The Anchorage Daily News had beaten us to the punch,” said Lori Townsend, chief editor and senior vice president of journalism at Alaska Public Media, which provides radio and television programming to public stations across the state. The organization, said Ms. Townsend, has taken to sharing content with its erstwhile competitors and co-hosts a political debate series with two other news organizations.

Detractors of the trend include Suzanne Downing, a former speechwriter and conservative journalist. “You’ll see the same stories,” said Ms. Downing, who now runs the news site The Alaska Story. “I’m not going to run Alaska Beacon stories. You can find that anywhere.”

There are limits to how far the cooperation can go. Four news organizations recently tried to organize a series of political debates, but the partnership fizzled after news consumers objected to past coverage from one of the outlets.

Scarcity is driving the pooling of resources among Alaska media companies. The same trends that have reduced newsrooms in other states have ravaged the Alaska press corps. Whereas The Associated Press once had a team of several reporters covering the state, it now has one. The Anchorage Daily News had a newsroom of more than 100 journalists decades ago and now has about 25. The Fairbanks Daily News-Miner has scaled back from a newsroom of 35 journalists a few decades ago to five these days.

The Juneau Empire, once a news anchor in the state capital, has shriveled into something shy of its grandiloquent banner. The paper’s owners whittled down the newsroom until its top editor, Mark Sabbatini, had no one left to supervise at one point.

“I didn’t want to be the person responsible for the paper ceasing to exist,” said Mr. Sabbatini, who later left The Empire and launched The Juneau Independent, a digital start-up.

Public radio has also suffered personnel and programming cutbacks stemming from the rollback of state and federal funding, according to Mollie Kabler, executive director of CoastAlaska, a nonprofit that serves public media operations in the state.

The situation, said Dermot Cole, a former columnist for The News-Miner, is dire. “It’s really showing up when we have something as important as this Senate race and it’s not being covered wall to wall,” he said.

The Alaskan bush also conspires against immersive campaign reporting. About 80 percent of communities in the state are not on the road system. Following candidates from one remote village to another, which requires air travel, is a budgetary no-go for Alaskan news organizations.

“I have not heard of anyone doing that for several election cycles,” said Julie Stricker, top editor at The News-Miner, noting that such travel is “prohibitively expensive.”

“None of the ‘Boys on the Bus’ stuff,” she added, referring to an iconic book about the reporters chronicling the 1972 presidential campaign.

Mid-October found Ms. Peltola hopping from one remote community to another in an effort “to reach every village, every voter.” “I thought she’d stick closer to the Railbelt,” Mr. Brooks said, referring to Alaska’s main population cluster. “But nope, and we can’t follow her there.”

Nor does it help that candidates for federal office in Alaska, like their peers elsewhere, appear to have less and less use for journalists. Liz Ruskin, the Washington correspondent for Alaska Public Media, said both main Senate candidates are “running multimillion-dollar campaigns and don’t see the need to talk to reporters as much.”

Evan Erickson, news director for KYUK, a nonprofit public media organization, requested an interview with Ms. Peltola this year when she made a swing through Bethel, a western Alaska city that’s home to KYUK and a hometown of the candidate. The campaign declined the request, so Mr. Erickson made his pitch directly to Ms. Peltola at a V.F.W. hall in front of her constituents, putting her in “that awkward position,” Mr. Erickson recalled. That did the trick.

Both campaigns defended their candidates’ availability to the news media. Nate Adams, a spokesman for the Sullivan campaign, said in a statement, “If our state’s newsrooms put out reporting Alaskans actually wanted, they wouldn’t need to pool their resources just to keep the lights on.”

Some stories, however, are just too big to run in just a single publication. Amy Bushatz, founder and publisher of The Mat-Su Sentinel, a digital news outlet north of Anchorage, licenses her coverage to The Anchorage Daily News for a monthly fee of $600. Among the recent articles that the regional daily republished was a detailed piece on a 122.7-pound cabbage that won the 30th annual Alaska State Fair Cabbage Weigh-Off.

It was the largest winning cabbage in more than a decade. “I mean, listen,” Ms. Bushatz said. “Don’t knock the cabbage.”

Georgia Gee contributed research.

item.title: In France, Raging Against the Luxury Machine
item.description:
Amid all of the images and videos that emerged of the riots that took place in France over the weekend, the most shocking are those of the clock tower collapsing in Limoges after its 19th-century town hall was set alight.

Close behind, however, are the shots of looters storming the gates of luxury brands like Celine, Hermès, Louis Vuitton and Saint Laurent, breaking through the plate-glass windows that act as a scrim between the outside world and the hushed interiors that cater to the ultrarich, smashing their sparkling vitrines and looting their goods.

Of the estimated more than 3,000 shops that have been affected by the spiraling protests, including grocery stores, pharmacies and family-run operations, it is the luxury destruction that has caught much of the attention, and the imagination, of the watching world.

Whenever demonstrations are coupled with looting, they set off a conversation about wider, often inchoate, expressions of anger over inequality, not just in France but across the world. And though it would be easy to see this as yet another blip in a long history of using luxury products as a stand-in for social and economic injustice (one that stretches back to the French Revolution), it is also a response to a peculiarly contemporary reality the luxury industry itself has created.

The current situation is, after all, the third instance of physical attacks against luxury brands in the last eight years in the city that has styled itself the capital of luxury. In 2023, during the movement against government pension reform, protesters stormed the doors of the LVMH headquarters on Avenue Montaigne in Paris, waving sparklers and ultimately burning an effigy of Bernard Arnault, the billionaire owner of the group (and that year briefly the richest man in the world).

In 2019, Dior and Chanel shops on the Champs-Élysées in Paris, among other luxury emporiums, were looted during demonstrations by the Gilets Jaunes (Yellow Vests), and boarded-up storefronts became a familiar sight.

According to Serge Carreira, the director of the emerging brands initiative at the Fédération de la Haute Couture and an affiliated professor at the School of Management and Impact at Sciences Po, “France has always cultivated a love-hate relationship with luxury — proud of its global influence, suspicious of its morality and blaming its unequal essence.”

In some ways, it is exactly that influence, so assiduously cultivated by the brands themselves, that is now backfiring.

Luxury has used social media and its own cultural cachet to make itself ubiquitous in the lives of even those who can’t afford its products. Thanks to celebrity ambassadors, the transformation of fashion shows into entertainment and the red carpet into a marketing opportunity, everybody knows Dior, even if they will never buy a Dior. Ditto Louis Vuitton, Chanel, Burberry and more.

(Ironically, the weekend protests coincided with LVMH’s Journées Particulières, or Open Days, an initiative in which many of the group’s brands welcome the public into their ateliers and workshops, to share how the products are made and invite consumers into their otherwise closed world.)

But paradoxically, as these brands have held themselves up as the epitome of aspiration and taste, they have also raised their prices to such levels that they are out of reach for almost everyone. They are emotionally and psychologically seductive but practically unattainable. As a result, “most of the younger generation feels excluded from this world,”Carreira said. “There is no more dream, just envy and rage.”

Those feelings found their expression in physical annihilation. By destroying the display windows of the opulent stores, Carreira said, the protesters are destroying a system that dangles only the promise of inclusion. “They escape the norm and reach a form of materialistic fulfillment,” he said.

By appropriating the products themselves, many of which have ended up on the luxury resale and black markets, the looters seized some of what had been otherwise denied them and literally brought it out to the street.

In this context, rather than being symbols of artisanship and patrimony, as luxury brands tend to describe themselves and their offerings, their goods become emblems of excess and capitalist rot.

As far as what will happen next, Dior, Celine and Hermès either did not respond to requests for comment, declined to comment on what happened with their stores or did not say what measures they had taken to protect them. Ralph Lauren did not respond to emails.

An internal note sent to LVMH employees on Oct. 19 by Antoine Arnault, the group head of communications and sustainability, and seen by The New York Times, noted that the group had “taken the appropriate measures to ensure everyone’s safety and the continuity of our operations.” (Reportedly, private security has been hired.) He also thanked the “artisans, virtuosos and all members of our teams,” calling them “our finest ambassadors.”

As curfews are imposed in France and cities gear up for another round of protests, the government is promising increased security. “I believe Avenue Montaigne and Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré will be Fort Knox next weekend and any other day of protest in the next weeks,” Carreira said.

Billionaires famously love a bunker, but do the brands that serve them really want to be stuck inside?
